query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: When deformed dynamically, the solid‐solution Co–free FeNiCrMn HEA shifts from thermally activated dislocation glide to a regime dominated by phonon drag—that is, as strain rates increase into the high-rate dynamic range and temperatures become sufficiently elevated, dislocation mobility is increasingly retarded by interactions with lattice vibrations. In the Co–free alloy, the altered phonon spectrum owing to the absence of Co leads to a larger increase in yield strength and more pronounced serrated flow characteristic of dynamic strain aging compared with the quasi‐static state.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully solidified, single-phase (solid-solution) FeNiCrMn HEA (derived from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy with Co removed) with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Application of deformation over a controlled range of strain rates, from slow, quasi-static conditions to high-rate dynamic loading, at selected temperatures.
generation.conditions: Testing should be performed in the regime where dislocation-mediated plasticity is active but before significant dynamic recrystallization or phase transformations occur; that is, at moderate to elevated temperatures and across strain rate regimes from quasi-static to high dynamic rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of dislocations interacting with lattice vibrations (phonons), as revealed by the presence and amplitude of serrated stress–strain responses.
generation.mechanism: At low strain rates, dislocations have sufficient time for thermal activation to overcome obstacles, leading to conventional glide; however, at high strain rates the limited deformation time enhances phonon drag effects, impeding dislocation motion. In the Co–free HEA, the removal of Co and the resulting modification of the local bonding and phonon spectrum amplifies this drag, causing an abrupt increase in yield strength and more pronounced serrated flow associated with dynamic strain aging.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quasi-static baseline, under dynamic loading (e.g., above 10³ s⁻¹) the Co–free alloy will exhibit a sharper increase in yield strength and larger amplitude serrations in the flow stress curves. This behavior should be more distinct than in a similar alloy with Co present.
generation.baseline: Quasi-static deformation conditions (<10⁻² s⁻¹) in which dislocation glide dominates, yielding relatively lower yield strength and minimal serrated flow.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase, as-solidified HEAs without interference from dynamic recrystallization or phase transformations. It is valid over the temperature range where phonon drag is effective (e.g., room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures) and for strain rate regimes where phonon drag begins to dominate over pure thermal activation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of the modified phonon spectrum due to the absence of Co is not yet fully characterized. Additionally, while phonon drag is a plausible explanation, other effects (e.g., minor solute interactions) may also contribute; thus, precise size of the effect remains uncertain without further atomistic or microstructural studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the Co–free FeNiCrMn HEA and, for a controlled comparison, a Co–containing CoCrFeMnNi HEA with similar processing history. Conduct a series of compression/tensile experiments (for example, using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar) at a range of strain rates spanning quasi-static (<10⁻² s⁻¹) to high dynamic (>10³ s⁻¹) conditions at a controlled temperature (in the regime where phonon drag is expected). Record full stress–strain responses, paying special attention to yield strength values and serration features.
measurements: Stress–strain curves and yield strength determination
Serration amplitude and frequency analysis in dynamic tests
Estimation of activation volumes from strain-rate sensitivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain rate tests do not reveal a marked increase in yield strength relative to quasi-static conditions, or if the amplitude and frequency of serrations do not significantly differ from the baseline, then the phonon drag–dominated mechanism is not supported. Additionally, if the Co–free and Co–containing alloys show indistinguishable dynamic behavior in this regime, the role of Co removal (and hence the modified phonon drag) would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. The Constitutive Model and Strain-Rate Sensitivity
cited_evidence.text: The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had positive activation volume at strain rates less than 1 × 10−2 s−1. However, when the specimen deformed under high strain rates (beyond 1 × 103 s−1), the deformation time was very short. There was not enough time available for thermal energy to help dislocations overcome the barriers. The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had a different deformation mechanism at dynamic loading. According to the literature [], the large jump in yield strength at high strain rates is probably due to the phonon drag effect on the motion of dislocations. The phonon drag phenomenon becomes very effective during plastic deformation at high strain rates []. A phonon is an elastic lattice vibration propagating in a crystal []. The viscous drag generating from the interaction of the dislocations has negative impacts on the deformation progress. The drag effects by the phonons can be ignored under quasi-static conditions for low dislocation velocities. However, high dislocation velocities under high strain rates would enhance the phonon drag effects greatly and lead to phonons scattering, which also hinders dislocation movement. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.2. Mechanism for the Serration Behavior
cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys present serrations on the flow stress curves during the plastic deformation, often at a normal strain rate around 1 × 10−4 s−1 or at low temperatures. Serration behavior exhibits in the stress-strain curves of the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy at 7 K, 7.5 K, and 9 K at a strain rate of 4 × 10−4 s−1 []. The Al5Cr12Fe35Mn28Ni20 high-entropy alloy exhibits typical serration behaviors at the elevated temperatures of 573 K and 673 K, with a strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1 []. Several microstructure mechanisms are proposed to explain the serration behavior, e.g., the Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect. Serration behavior was supposed to be associated with Cottrell atmosphere interaction with moving dislocations, slip bands, and dynamic strain aging. In Figure 4, it can be seen that the stress-strain curves of the as-cast NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 show no serrations, and marked serrations are present on the stress-strain curves of specimens deformed at strain rates above 900 s−1.
